elements.content:
Most restaurant owners I talk to still treat their website like a digital brochure. Then they wonder why guests keep calling in or opening a delivery app instead.

Owner, a restaurant platform, recently published its 2026 guide to online ordering systems. Two numbers stood out to me. It says 58% of customers prefer ordering delivery through a restaurant's own website or app. It also reports checkout completion around 8% on its platform versus about 4.5% on the average restaurant site. That's vendor data, so I'd treat it as a direction rather than a benchmark.

Still, the direction matches what I see on the ground. A guest who can order from their phone in a few taps, without landing on a dead page, is a guest you keep. Every extra screen at checkout is someone who quietly leaves for a competitor.

If you want a quick test, order from your own site on your phone tonight. Time it. Count the taps. Then fix the slowest step first.

elements.content:
A 4.6-star restaurant was losing customers to its own Google profile.
Sensaciones is an elevated Cuban restaurant in Fort Myers. The chef has 16+ years in high-end kitchens. The food is the real deal.
But they moved into a location where another restaurant used to be. And their Google profile was still showing that other business: old photos, even pictures of frozen product packages.
Someone searching "Cuban restaurant" saw that and kept scrolling.
3 signs your profile is working against you:
→ Photos that aren't yours (old business, packaging, blurry shots)
→ Name, address or phone that don't match across Google, Bing and directories
→ A generic category, without the words people actually search
What we did:
→ Removed the old photos and added a new professional gallery
→ Made the info match on Google and Bing
→ Set the right categories and keywords
→ Built a new website with WhatsApp reservations
30 days later, compared to the month before:
→ +77.1% clicks to the menu
→ +52.2% direction requests
→ +21.9% mobile searches
→ Top 3 for "Cuban restaurant" in Fort Myers
Take 2 minutes today: search your business on Google Maps. Do you see any of the 3 signs?

That's the clearest way I've found to explain self-order kiosks to hospitality owners. A tired team member on the 50th order of a lunch rush will sometimes forget to offer chips with that. The sensible test: trial one beside your till for a busy month and judge the numbers.

elements.content:
Ipsos sent mystery shoppers on 2,772 mobile orders across 40 quick service brands and surveyed 1,700 customers about what they care about. Nation's Restaurant News published the results on 16 October.

Order accuracy came first, at 92%. Food that tastes the same in the bag as in the store came next, at 85%, then the right temperature, at 84%. Perks like reordering past favorites ranked lower.

Every one of those is decided in the kitchen and at the pickup shelf of one particular store. The app is the same everywhere. The bag is not.

That makes the gap hard to see from head office. A brand average of 4.4 stars can hide three stores that keep forgetting the sauce.

Run a two-question survey after each pickup, read it store by store, and you find those three before the one-star reviews do.

Habit Burger & Grill is giving away 200,000 free meals over 10 days, October 26 through November 4, through a campaign it’s calling Habit Hour. The first 50 guests at each participating restaurant during a one-hour window get a $10 Gotta Habit Dipping Trio Box. It’s no purchase required, but you have to order in person at the register, so drive-thru, app, and online orders don’t count. That works out to 500 meals per restaurant and roughly $2 million in food.

The time changes every day. MyHabit members with push notifications on get a heads-up two hours before, and the exact start is revealed on social one hour before. CEO Shannon Hennessy said it started with the question, “What if we just gave people dinner?” Recipients are also asked to do a simple act of kindness of their own, which the brand calls Pay Good Forward.

A surprise window with an in-person requirement puts a line at the register of every participating restaurant, and the restaurant owns what happens once those 50 people are inside.

elements.content:
McDonald's brought the McRib back today. "Select locations." "Check the app." Some stores already had it last week.

That's fine when you're McDonald's.

When you run a handful of restaurants, that's how you lose a regular.

You post the fall special on Instagram Monday. Tuesday a guest drives to your second location and asks for it. The server has never heard of it. The manager didn't get the email. The menu on Google still says summer.

The guest doesn't blame the server. They decide your marketing lies.

That's what working across Hibernian's 23+ North Carolina concepts keeps teaching me. More locations doesn't mean more marketing. It means more places for one message to break.

Here's what a hospitality marketing system actually looks like:

One calendar every location sees before anything goes public.
A launch date per store, not a vague "rolling out soon."
The GM signs off that the kitchen can make it before the post goes up.
Google profile, website menu and third-party listings updated the same day.
A one-line script for the host stand so the answer is the same everywhere.

Don't:
Let each location run its own Instagram with its own promos.
Announce something the kitchen hasn't tested on a Friday night.
Treat the website menu as a someday task.
Measure the launch by likes when you should be checking if covers moved.

The ad isn't the hard part. Making every door match the ad is.

I wrote up the full approach here: https://lnkd.in/eKTu7dP5

This week, call your own second location and ask about your newest special. Whatever they say is what your guests are hearing.
